choices: The instance (SGA + background processes) crashed, but the database (datafiles, redo, control files on disk) is intact — restart the instance; crash recovery replays redo automatically
The database is corrupted; restore from backup
Datafiles are gone when the instance dies
Restarting is unsafe; rebuild the database
scenarios.hint: Which parts of 'the database' live in memory, and which live on disk?
scenarios.prompt: What actually failed, and what is the recovery action?
scenarios.situation: A power outage kills the server. The DBA says 'the instance is down but the database is fine.' A manager hears 'database is fine' and asks why anything needs doing.
scenarios.title: The power outage
scenarios.why: Instance = memory (SGA) + background processes; database = physical files (datafiles, control files, redo logs). A crash loses the instance, not the files. On startup, Oracle performs automatic crash recovery: SMON rolls forward committed changes from redo and rolls back uncommitted ones. No backup restore is needed — that's the whole point of redo logging.

choices: DBWn (database writer) — writes dirty buffers to datafiles, lazily; LGWR (log writer) writes redo on commit — which is why commit is fast and datafiles can lag
LGWR writes datafiles; DBWn writes redo
CKPT writes user data on every commit
scenarios.hint: Which process must act before a commit returns, and which one can afford to be lazy?
scenarios.prompt: Which background processes handle the commit path, and why is commit fast?
scenarios.situation: A developer is surprised that COMMIT returns in milliseconds even with megabytes of changes, yet the datafiles aren't updated for minutes.
scenarios.title: The fast commit
scenarios.why: LGWR writes the redo log buffer to disk on every commit (sequential, fast) — that's the durability guarantee. DBWn writes dirty data buffers lazily in batches (random I/O, deferred). This write-ahead logging means: commit is fast because only redo is forced; datafiles catch up later. CKPT just records checkpoints; ARCn archives redo logs.

choices: PGA — private per-session memory for sorts, hashes, and cursor state; SGA is shared (buffer cache, shared pool, redo buffer)
SGA — each session gets its own SGA
PGA is shared across sessions for efficiency
Sorts happen in datafiles, not memory
scenarios.hint: Which memory area is per-server-process, and which is shared by all?
scenarios.prompt: Where does a large sort consume memory, and what is shared vs private?
scenarios.situation: A big ORDER BY spills to temp. The DBA increases PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET and explains SGA vs PGA to the team.
scenarios.title: The spilling sort
scenarios.why: SGA (System Global Area) is shared: buffer cache, shared pool (parsed SQL, dictionary cache), redo log buffer. PGA (Program Global Area) is per-server-process: sort areas, hash areas, session cursor state. Large sorts/hashes consume PGA; when PGA is insufficient they spill to TEMP. Sizing: SGA for caching, PGA for per-session work areas.

choices: Control files — they record the database structure, datafile locations, checkpoint SCNs, and RMAN metadata; multiplex them on separate disks
Parameter files — they list the control files
Redo logs — they store the schema
The alert log — it has the structure
scenarios.hint: If you lost every copy of this file, could Oracle even find its datafiles?
scenarios.prompt: Which file is the database's 'table of contents,' and how is it protected?
scenarios.situation: A DBA insists control files live on three separate disks. A manager calls it paranoia — 'we have backups of everything anyway.'
scenarios.title: The three control files
scenarios.why: The control file is the database's metadata hub: datafile/tempfile locations, log sequence numbers, checkpoint SCN, RMAN repository info. Lose all copies and the instance can't mount — recovery becomes a rebuild-from-backup exercise. Multiplexing (multiple copies on independent storage) is cheap insurance; it's standard, not paranoia.

choices: CDB (container) holds the root and seed; PDBs (pluggable databases) are portable, self-contained databases sharing one instance — unplug/plug for moves, patch once at CDB level
PDBs are just schemas with a new name
Multitenant requires a separate license for every PDB in all editions
scenarios.hint: Which architecture lets you unplug a whole database and plug it into another container?
scenarios.prompt: What is the multitenant architecture, and what operational problem does it solve?
scenarios.situation: A company runs 40 small databases — 40 instances, 40 patch cycles, 40 memory footprints. They ask about consolidation.
scenarios.title: The forty databases
scenarios.why: Multitenant: one CDB (container database) hosts many PDBs (pluggable databases), sharing one instance/SGA/background processes. Benefits: patch/upgrade once at CDB level, unplug/plug PDBs to move them between CDBs, clone via snapshot. Each PDB looks like a standalone database to applications. It's the consolidation answer for 'many small databases'.

choices: Undo tablespace — stores before-images for read consistency and rollback; too-small undo causes ORA-01555 snapshot too old on long queries
System tablespace — undo lives in SYSTEM
Undo is only needed for failed transactions
scenarios.hint: Where does Oracle keep the 'before' picture that a long-running query reads?
scenarios.prompt: What causes ORA-01555, and which tablespace is involved?
scenarios.situation: A 2-hour report fails with ORA-01555 'snapshot too old' while heavy updates run concurrently.
scenarios.title: The snapshot too old
scenarios.why: Read consistency: a query sees data as of its start SCN, reconstructed from undo (before-images) when blocks changed underneath it. If undo is overwritten before the query finishes → ORA-01555. Fixes: size undo tablespace + undo retention appropriately, tune the long query, or reduce concurrent churn. Undo also rolls back uncommitted transactions — it's the backbone of MVCC.

scenarios.title: The abort
scenarios.situation: DBA uses SHUTDOWN ABORT nightly.
choices: Forces crash recovery every time — use IMMEDIATE
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. ABORT is crash-consistent shutdown — routine use forces recovery every startup.

scenarios.title: The LGWR wait
scenarios.situation: Log file sync waits dominate.
choices: Commit latency — LGWR/IO is the bottleneck
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'log file sync' = waiting on commit — storage or LGWR tuning.

choices: DBCA (Database Configuration Assistant) — GUI/silent, handles prerequisites, templates, and post-creation config; manual CREATE DATABASE is for edge cases needing full control
Manual SQL scripts are the only supported method
scenarios.hint: Which tool encodes Oracle's own best-practice creation steps?
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard creation path, and when would you go manual?
scenarios.situation: A junior DBA wants to hand-write CREATE DATABASE scripts 'to learn'. The lead says use DBCA for production.
scenarios.title: The creation debate
scenarios.why: DBCA is the supported, standard path: it validates prerequisites, applies templates (including CDB/PDB, sample schemas), sets parameters sensibly, and configures listeners/EM. Manual creation (CREATE DATABASE script) is for unusual cases — learning internals, or custom layouts DBCA can't express. Production: DBCA (silent mode for automation); learning: manual once, to understand what DBCA does.

choices: OS prerequisites: oracle user/groups, kernel parameters (shared memory, semaphores), sufficient RAM/swap, and proper filesystem layout — installers fail or databases misbehave without them
Kernel parameters are set automatically on all platforms
scenarios.hint: What does the installer check before it even starts copying files?
scenarios.prompt: What prerequisite class causes most installation failures?
scenarios.situation: An Oracle install fails midway with shared-memory errors. The sysadmin skipped the preinstall RPM and kernel settings.
scenarios.title: The failed install
scenarios.why: Oracle has hard OS prerequisites: the oracle user and groups (oinstall, dba), kernel parameters for shared memory/semaphores (SHMMAX, SEMMNS etc.), package dependencies, and ulimits. The preinstall RPM (oracle-database-preinstall) automates most of this on Oracle Linux. Skipping them produces cryptic mid-install failures — check prerequisites first, always.

choices: Choose it at creation — changing character sets later (especially to/from multibyte) is painful and sometimes requires full export/import; AL32UTF8 is the modern default
Character sets can be changed anytime with ALTER DATABASE
NLS settings don't affect stored data
scenarios.hint: Can you ALTER a database from WE8ISO8859P1 to AL32UTF8 after it has data?
scenarios.prompt: Why is character set choice a creation-time decision?
scenarios.situation: A database created with a single-byte character set now needs emoji and CJK data. The team discovers conversion options are limited and risky.
scenarios.title: The emoji problem
scenarios.why: The database character set determines how text is stored; changing it after data exists ranges from restricted (CSSCAN/CSALTER for compatible supersets) to full export/import. AL32UTF8 (Unicode) is the safe modern default — it stores everything. Getting this wrong at creation is a multi-week migration later.

choices: Initialization parameters (SPFILE/PFILE): MEMORY_TARGET/SGA_TARGET, PROCESSES, DB_BLOCK_SIZE (set at creation), COMPATIBLE, UNDO settings — and know which are dynamic vs static
Parameters are all dynamic; restart is never needed
scenarios.hint: Which parameters demand a restart, and which is frozen at creation?
scenarios.prompt: What parameter knowledge does a DBA need on day one?
scenarios.situation: A new DBA changes DB_BLOCK_SIZE in the SPFILE and bounces the instance — startup fails.
scenarios.title: The unstartable instance
scenarios.why: DB_BLOCK_SIZE is set at database creation and immutable after. Parameters live in the SPFILE (binary, server-side, persistent) or PFILE (text, client-side); ALTER SYSTEM SET ... SCOPE=MEMORY/SPFILE/BOTH controls persistence, and some parameters are static (restart required). Know the critical ones: memory targets, PROCESSES (connection ceiling), COMPATIBLE, undo retention — and which need a bounce.

choices: Verify: instance open, listener serving, basic connectivity, alert log clean, backup scheduled, and a test restore — creation isn't done until recovery is proven
Creation success message is sufficient proof
Backups can wait until next quarter
The alert log is only for errors
scenarios.hint: What proves the database is actually operable, not just created?
scenarios.prompt: What does 'done' look like after creating a database?
scenarios.situation: DBCA reports success. The DBA wants to hand over to the app team immediately.
scenarios.title: The handover checklist
scenarios.why: A created database isn't a production database until: it opens cleanly after a bounce, the listener accepts connections, the alert log shows no errors, ARCHIVELOG mode + RMAN backups are configured and a test restore succeeded, and monitoring covers it. 'DBCA said success' is step one of ten.

choices: Silent/response-file installs and DBCA templates — identical, repeatable, version-controlled builds; GUI installs are for one-offs
Automation isn't possible for Oracle installs
scenarios.hint: How do you build the 11th identical database exactly like the first 10?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make database builds repeatable?
scenarios.situation: A team must build 10 identical dev databases. Manual GUI installs drift within the third build.
scenarios.title: The drifting builds
scenarios.why: Response files (silent install) and DBCA templates make builds deterministic: same parameters, same options, every time — and they're version-controllable. GUI installs are fine for a single learning build; fleets need automation. Record the response file alongside the build docs.

scenarios.title: The snowflake
scenarios.situation: Each install done differently.
choices: Response files + version control — repeatable installs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Standardized silent installs eliminate snowflakes.

scenarios.title: The unpatched
scenarios.situation: No RUs in 18 months.
choices: Known CVEs unpatched — quarterly routine required
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Patch debt is vulnerability debt — the quarterly routine exists for a reason.

choices: SYSTEM holds the data dictionary (never put user data there); SYSAUX holds auxiliary metadata (AWR, EM); UNDO holds before-images; TEMP holds sort/hash spill — each has a distinct failure/space behavior
User tables go in SYSTEM for speed
scenarios.hint: Which tablespace would break the data dictionary if it filled with user tables?
scenarios.prompt: What are the mandatory tablespaces and their roles?
scenarios.situation: A developer creates tables in SYSTEM 'because it's the default'. The DBA calls it a critical finding.
scenarios.title: The SYSTEM squatter
scenarios.why: SYSTEM = data dictionary (Oracle's own metadata) — user objects there risk dictionary corruption and upgrade failures. SYSAUX = auxiliary repository (AWR snapshots, OEM data). UNDO = transaction before-images. TEMP = sort/hash spillover. Each has different space pressure symptoms: SYSTEM full = can't do DDL; TEMP full = big queries fail; UNDO full = DML stalls. Keep user data in dedicated tablespaces.

choices: AUTOEXTEND with MAXSIZE + monitoring/alerts on tablespace usage — growth is handled, runaway growth is capped and visible
Disable AUTOEXTEND everywhere and extend manually at 3 AM
One giant datafile per tablespace is best practice
Space alerts are unnecessary with AUTOEXTEND
scenarios.hint: Which combination grows automatically but can't grow forever unnoticed?
scenarios.situation: A tablespace hits 100% at 2 AM and transactions fail. AUTOEXTEND was off 'to control growth'.
scenarios.title: The full tablespace
scenarios.why: AUTOEXTEND ON with a sensible MAXSIZE lets datafiles grow with demand while capping runaway growth (a bad load can't fill the disk). Pair it with usage alerts (e.g., 80/90% thresholds via EM or scripts) so growth is visible before it becomes an outage. Manual-only extension trades control for 2 AM pages.

choices: ASM (Automatic Storage Management) — Oracle-managed striping/mirroring across disks with rebalance; filesystem storage is simpler but you manage layout/redundancy yourself
Filesystems are always faster than ASM
scenarios.hint: Which storage layer stripes and mirrors for the database automatically?
scenarios.prompt: When does ASM win over plain filesystem storage?
scenarios.situation: A DBA must choose storage for a production database on direct-attached disks, wanting striping and mirroring without manual volume management.
scenarios.title: The storage layer choice
scenarios.why: ASM is Oracle's volume manager/filesystem: it stripes data across disks, mirrors per failure group, and rebalances online when disks are added/removed. Filesystem (or NFS/dNFS) storage is simpler and fine for many cases, but striping/mirroring/redundancy become your problem. ASM doesn't replace backups — mirroring protects against disk failure, not against DROP TABLE.

choices: Segment → extents → blocks: a segment (table/index) is made of extents (contiguous block groups), each extent of Oracle blocks; locally managed tablespaces with AUTOALLOCATE handle this automatically
scenarios.hint: Which is smallest: block, extent, or segment?
scenarios.prompt: What is the logical-to-physical storage hierarchy?
scenarios.situation: A junior DBA is confused by 'segment', 'extent', and 'block' in space reports.
scenarios.title: The space vocabulary
scenarios.why: Block (smallest, e.g., 8 KB) → extent (set of contiguous blocks allocated at once) → segment (the table/index/partition's extents) → tablespace → datafile. Locally managed tablespaces (the modern default) track this in bitmaps; AUTOALLOCATE sizes extents automatically. Understanding the hierarchy is what makes space reports readable.

choices: Bigfile tablespaces (single large datafile, up to 128 TB) simplify management for very large databases; smallfile (classic, many datafiles) suits most cases — choose by scale
Bigfile is mandatory for all databases
scenarios.hint: One huge datafile vs many smaller ones — which simplifies a 50 TB tablespace?
scenarios.prompt: When do bigfile tablespaces make sense?
scenarios.situation: A 40 TB warehouse needs a new tablespace. The DBA debates bigfile vs smallfile.
scenarios.title: The 40 TB tablespace
scenarios.why: Bigfile tablespaces use one datafile (up to ~128 TB depending on block size) — fewer files to manage, ideal for very large databases and ASM. Smallfile (traditional, up to 1024 datafiles per tablespace) is the default and fine for typical sizes. It's a manageability/scale choice, invisible to SQL.

choices: Proactive: trend usage, alert at thresholds, add space before exhaustion; reactive: add datafile/resize on failure — and know that some objects (e.g., in SYSTEM) can't wait
scenarios.hint: Which tablespace filling is a 2 AM page, and which is a next-week task?
scenarios.prompt: What is the operational discipline for space?
scenarios.situation: UNDO tablespace fills during a huge batch; TEMP fills during month-end reports. Both cause failures, but the responses differ.
scenarios.title: The space triage
scenarios.why: Not all 'full' is equal: SYSTEM/SYSAUX full blocks DDL and can wedge the database (page now); TEMP full fails the big queries using it (add tempfile or tune the query); UNDO full stalls DML (add space or reduce batch commit scope). Discipline: trend growth, alert at 80/90%, and know the per-tablespace playbook — ADD DATAFILE/RESIZE is online.

scenarios.title: The SYSTEM data
scenarios.situation: App tables in SYSTEM.
choices: Move to dedicated tablespaces — SYSTEM is Oracle's
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. User objects don't belong in SYSTEM — move them out.

scenarios.title: The 01555
scenarios.situation: ORA-01555 snapshot too old.
choices: Size undo for the longest query — retention tuning
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. ORA-01555 means undo couldn't cover the query's duration — size up.

choices: ARCHIVELOG mode — redo is archived instead of overwritten, enabling point-in-time recovery; NOARCHIVELOG only allows restore to the last backup with data loss
NOARCHIVELOG is fine for production; backups are enough
ARCHIVELOG mode slows down commits unacceptably
The modes are identical for recovery
scenarios.hint: What happens to a redo log when it fills — overwritten, or saved?
scenarios.prompt: Why is ARCHIVELOG mode non-negotiable for production?
scenarios.situation: A production database runs in NOARCHIVELOG. A disk failure at 2 PM destroys datafiles; the last backup was midnight. The business asks: 'Can we get back to 1:59 PM?'
scenarios.title: The 2 PM failure
scenarios.why: In NOARCHIVELOG, filled redo logs are overwritten — the transactions between midnight and 2 PM are unrecoverable. ARCHIVELOG preserves each filled log (ARCn copies it out), so RMAN can restore the midnight backup and roll forward through archived logs to 1:59 PM. That's point-in-time recovery, and it's why production runs ARCHIVELOG.

choices: Restore = copy backup files back to their locations; Recover = apply redo/archived logs to roll forward to the target time — you almost always do both
Recover copies files; restore applies logs
Only one of them is ever needed
scenarios.hint: Which step puts the files back, and which step replays history onto them?
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference between restore and recover?
scenarios.situation: A runbook says 'restore the database' and the junior DBA copies files back, then opens the database — it's inconsistent and won't open.
scenarios.title: The half recovery
scenarios.why: RESTORE copies backup pieces to datafile locations (files as of backup time). RECOVER applies archived/incremental changes to roll them forward to the desired point. Skipping RECOVER leaves files at backup-time SCN — inconsistent with the control file, so the database won't open. RMAN's RECOVER DATABASE does the roll-forward; then OPEN RESETLOGS if recovery was incomplete.

choices: Incremental strategy: weekly level-0 + daily level-1 (differential or cumulative) — faster backups, reasonable restore chains; validate with RESTORE VALIDATE and periodic test restores
Full backup every night — simplest, always best
Cumulative incrementals don't exist in RMAN
scenarios.hint: What backs up only changed blocks, and how do you prove the backups work?
scenarios.prompt: What is a sane RMAN backup strategy, and how is it proven?
scenarios.situation: A 5 TB database does full backups nightly — the window is blown. Nobody has ever test-restored.
scenarios.title: The blown backup window
scenarios.why: RMAN incremental backups (level 0 base + level 1 changed-blocks-only; differential = since last level-1, cumulative = since last level-0) shrink the nightly window dramatically. Block change tracking makes incrementals fast. And backups are Schrödinger's backups until tested: RESTORE VALIDATE checks readability, but only a real test restore proves recoverability. Untested backups are hopes, not plans.

choices: Flashback (FLASHBACK TABLE/DATABASE) for logical errors — rewinds to a before-image using undo/flashback logs, fast and online; media recovery (RMAN) is for physical loss
scenarios.hint: Dropped the wrong table at 10 AM — do you need the backup tapes, or the undo?
scenarios.prompt: When do you use Flashback vs RMAN media recovery?
scenarios.situation: Someone drops the ORDERS table at 10 AM (logical error). Separately: a disk dies (physical loss). The team reaches for RMAN for both.
scenarios.title: The dropped table
scenarios.why: Flashback rewinds logical mistakes using undo/flashback logs — FLASHBACK TABLE TO TIMESTAMP can resurrect the dropped table in minutes without a restore. RMAN media recovery rebuilds physically lost/damaged files from backups + redo. Rule: logical error (wrong DML, dropped object) → Flashback (fast, online); physical loss (dead disk, corrupt file) → RMAN restore + recover. (Recycle bin also saves dropped tables if not purged.)

choices: Retention policy (recovery window or redundancy) + archived-log deletion policy — RMAN knows what's obsolete and DELETE OBSOLETE cleans it; deleting OS files by hand corrupts the catalog
Delete old backup files with rm — RMAN notices automatically
Keep every backup forever — disk is cheap
scenarios.hint: If you rm a backup piece, what does the RMAN catalog still believe?
scenarios.prompt: How do you manage backup lifecycle without breaking RMAN?
scenarios.situation: The backup disk fills. An admin rm's old backup files; the next RMAN job fails with 'backup piece not found'.
scenarios.title: The full backup disk
scenarios.why: RMAN's catalog tracks every backup piece — OS-level deletes leave phantom catalog entries. Manage lifecycle inside RMAN: CONFIGURE RETENTION POLICY (recovery window of N days, or redundancy of N copies), then DELETE OBSOLETE / DELETE EXPIRED to clean catalog + files together. CROSSCHECK syncs the catalog with reality after any external change.

choices: Incomplete recovery: restore, recover until the last good log/time, then OPEN RESETLOGS — creating a new incarnation; document the divergence for the standby
Recover to the corrupted log — corruption is usually harmless
Resetlogs can be avoided by restoring twice
scenarios.hint: After recovering to a point before the end of redo, what must happen to the log sequence?
scenarios.prompt: What is incomplete recovery, and why does it end with RESETLOGS?
scenarios.situation: Archived logs are missing a 30-minute gap — recovery can only reach 1:30 PM, not the 2:00 PM failure point.
scenarios.title: The gap in the logs
scenarios.why: When you can't recover to the present (missing/corrupt logs), you do incomplete recovery: RESTORE, RECOVER UNTIL TIME/SEQUENCE, then OPEN RESETLOGS — which resets the log sequence and starts a new database incarnation. Consequences: take a fresh backup immediately (old backups belong to the prior incarnation), and Data Guard standbys need re-instantiation. RESETLOGS marks the timeline fork — it's deliberate, not a failure.

scenarios.title: The untested
scenarios.situation: Backups run; never restored.
choices: Untested backups are hopes — restore-drill on schedule
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The restore is the backup — drill it regularly.

scenarios.title: The no-archivelog
scenarios.situation: ARCHIVELOG off; PITR needed.
choices: Enable ARCHIVELOG — no logs, no point-in-time recovery
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. PITR requires archivelogs — NOARCHIVELOG means full-restore-only.

choices: AWR (Automatic Workload Repository) snapshots + ADDM findings, and ASH for second-by-second session history — start with wait events and top SQL, not guesses
Add indexes to every table — indexes always help
Increase SGA until the problem disappears
Restart the database; performance issues are usually transient
scenarios.hint: What tells you where time actually went, versus where you guess it went?
scenarios.prompt: What is the evidence-driven diagnosis path?
scenarios.situation: 'The database is slow' — the team wants to add indexes everywhere. Nobody has looked at AWR.
scenarios.title: The slow database
scenarios.why: Methodology: AWR snapshots capture workload stats over intervals; ADDM analyzes them and ranks findings; ASH samples active sessions every second for fine-grained 'who waited on what'. Read top wait events first (they name the bottleneck: db file sequential read = I/O, latch free = contention), then top SQL by elapsed time. Evidence before indexes.

choices: Stale or missing optimizer statistics — the optimizer's cost model depends on them; gather with DBMS_STATS and check LAST_ANALYZED; histograms matter for skewed columns
Statistics are only for the DBA's curiosity
Gathering stats always makes things worse
scenarios.hint: What does the optimizer base its cost estimates on?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most common cause of a suddenly-bad plan?
scenarios.situation: A query's plan flips overnight from an index range scan to a full table scan. Data volume barely changed. Stats were last gathered 6 months ago.
scenarios.title: The flipped plan
scenarios.why: The cost-based optimizer chooses plans from statistics (row counts, distinct values, histograms, index clustering). Stale stats → wrong costs → bad plans. DBMS_STATS.GATHER_* refreshes them; check DBA_TAB_STATISTICS.LAST_ANALYZED. Skewed columns need histograms or the optimizer assumes uniform distribution. Auto stats jobs usually handle this — verify they're actually running.

choices: Read the plan: operation order, access paths (full scan vs index), join methods, and the E-Rows vs A-Rows gap — a big gap means bad stats; DBMS_XPLAN shows it
Plans are unreadable; just try hints
The plan with the most steps is best
evidence: E-Rows=10, A-Rows=2,000,000 on the driving table
scenarios.hint: Estimated 10 rows, actual 2 million — what does that gap tell you?
scenarios.prompt: How do you read an execution plan for the smoking gun?
scenarios.situation: A query runs 100x slower than expected. DBMS_XPLAN shows E-Rows=10 vs A-Rows=2,000,000 on the driving table.
scenarios.title: The lying estimate
scenarios.why: The E-Rows/A-Rows gap is the classic smoking gun: the optimizer estimated 10 rows (nested loops looked cheap) but got 2M (nested loops = disaster). Root cause is almost always bad/missing stats or missing histograms. Fix the inputs (stats), not the plan — hints freeze a plan that may rot. Read plans inside-out: driving table, access path, join method, then row estimates.

choices: Wait events name the bottleneck: 'db file sequential read' = single-block I/O (index reads — check storage/index efficiency); 'log file sync' = commit latency (LGWR/storage); 'latch: cache buffers chains' = hot blocks (contention)
'Idle' waits are the ones to tune
scenarios.hint: Which waits represent real bottlenecks, and which are just sessions sitting idle?
scenarios.prompt: How do you translate top wait events into action?
scenarios.situation: AWR top waits: 'db file sequential read', 'log file sync', 'latch: cache buffers chains'. The team proposes adding CPUs.
scenarios.title: The wait-event readout
scenarios.why: Tune what you wait on: sequential read (single-block reads, often index-driven) → I/O subsystem or index/plan efficiency; log file sync → commit frequency and redo storage latency (batch commits, faster redo disk); cache-buffers-chains latch → hot blocks (partitioning, reverse-key indexes, reduce contention). Idle waits (SQL*Net message from client) are sessions waiting for the app — not tunable. CPUs help only if the top wait is CPU.

choices: Indexes speed reads but cost on DML (maintenance per insert/update/delete) and space — index selectively: high-selectivity WHERE/JOIN columns, and drop unused ones (monitor via index usage tracking)
Index every column — reads are all that matter
scenarios.hint: What happens on every INSERT when a table has 12 indexes?
scenarios.situation: A write-heavy table has 12 indexes 'for reporting'. Inserts are slow; reports use 3 of the indexes.
scenarios.title: The over-indexed table
scenarios.why: Every index is maintained on every DML — 12 indexes ≈ 12 extra writes per insert, plus space and slower stats gathering. Index the selective predicates that matter (WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY on high-cardinality columns); monitor usage (DBA_INDEX_USAGE / index monitoring) and drop the dead weight. Composite indexes serve multi-column predicates; function-based indexes serve expressions.

choices: Bind variables / cursor sharing — literals force a hard parse per distinct value (shared pool churn, latch contention); binds make SQL reusable
Cursor sharing is automatic for all literals
evidence: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345; -- 50k distinct literals/day
scenarios.hint: What happens in the shared pool when every execution has a different literal?
scenarios.prompt: Why is literal-heavy SQL a scalability killer?
scenarios.situation: An app concatenates values into SQL — 50k distinct statements/day. The shared pool churns, library-cache latches spike, CPU burns on parsing.
scenarios.title: The parse storm
scenarios.why: Each unique literal text is a new cursor: hard parse (syntax, optimize, load into shared pool) every time — CPU-intensive and latch-contended. Bind variables make the SQL text identical, so it's parsed once and reused (soft parses). CURSOR_SHARING=FORCE is a band-aid with plan-stability risks; fixing the app to bind is the cure. Parse once, execute many.

scenarios.title: The top wait
scenarios.situation: AWR top event: db file sequential read.
choices: Index IO waits — check indexing and storage latency
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Sequential reads = single-block index IO — tune indexes or storage.

scenarios.title: The plan flip
scenarios.situation: Good plan went bad overnight.
choices: SPM baseline — lock the known-good plan; check stats
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Plan instability needs baselines — capture good, enforce stable.

choices: Physical standby: block-for-block replica via redo apply — the DR copy; logical standby: SQL-apply replica, open read-write for reporting/offload — choose by whether you need an identical DR target or a usable reporting copy
Logical standby is the DR copy
scenarios.hint: Which one is a byte-identical copy, and which one is open for queries and reporting?
scenarios.prompt: What distinguishes physical from logical standby?
scenarios.situation: A team wants both disaster recovery and a reporting offload. They assume one standby does both.
scenarios.title: The two-standby question
scenarios.why: Physical standby = redo apply, block-identical, mounted (read-only with Active Data Guard) — the true DR replica for failover. Logical standby = SQL apply into open tables, read-write — usable for reporting and even rolling upgrades, but it's a logical reconstruction, not a block copy. One physical standby is the DR answer; add logical/ADG readers for offload.

choices: Switchover = planned role reversal (primary ↔ standby), no data loss, reversible; Failover = emergency promotion when primary is dead, potential data loss, standby becomes primary
Failover is planned; switchover is emergency
scenarios.hint: Which one do you schedule for maintenance, and which one do you trigger at 3 AM?
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference, and when is each used?
scenarios.situation: A planned datacenter maintenance needs the standby to take over with zero data loss. Separately, the team asks what happens if the primary datacenter burns down.
scenarios.title: The role transition
scenarios.why: Switchover: coordinated, both databases healthy — primary becomes standby and vice versa, zero data loss, used for maintenance/patching. Failover: primary is gone — promote the standby, accept possible data loss (depends on protection mode/sync), one-way. Test switchovers regularly; they're also your DR drill.

choices: Maximum Performance (async, no data-loss guarantee, minimal primary impact) → Maximum Availability (sync, zero loss unless standby unreachable, then async) → Maximum Protection (sync, zero loss guaranteed, primary stalls if standby lost)
The modes only affect speed, not data loss
Modes can't be changed after setup
scenarios.hint: Which mode can stall the primary to guarantee zero data loss?
scenarios.prompt: How do the three protection modes trade off?
scenarios.situation: A bank demands zero data loss; a SaaS company prioritizes primary performance. Both ask which mode.
scenarios.title: The zero-loss demand
scenarios.why: Max Performance: ASYNC redo — primary never waits, standby may lag (potential loss). Max Availability: SYNC — zero loss while standby is reachable; drops to async if the standby fails (primary keeps running). Max Protection: SYNC with guarantee — primary stalls rather than risk loss (highest safety, availability cost). Match the mode to the RPO: banks → availability/protection; latency-sensitive SaaS → performance.

choices: Redo transport lag / apply lag — query V$DATAGUARD_STATS or the broker's SHOW DATABASE; gaps come from network issues, standby downtime, or log deletion on primary before shipping
Delete archived logs aggressively to reduce lag
scenarios.hint: Which view shows 'how far behind is my standby, in time'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you detect and diagnose standby lag?
scenarios.situation: After a network blip, the team suspects the standby is behind but has no measurement.
scenarios.title: The silent gap
scenarios.why: Monitor transport lag (redo shipped vs generated) and apply lag (redo applied vs received) via V$DATAGUARD_STATS / Data Guard Broker. Gaps arise from network outages, standby downtime, or primary deleting logs before shipment (size the fast recovery area / set log deletion policies accordingly). FAL (fetch archive log) usually auto-resolves gaps — verify it did.

choices: Observer + Fast-Start Failover (FSFO) — automates detection and promotion within seconds when conditions are met; manual failover is the fallback
Automatic failover is the default in Data Guard
scenarios.hint: What component watches the primary and triggers promotion without a human?
scenarios.prompt: How do you automate failover, and what are the prerequisites?
scenarios.situation: RTO demands failover in under a minute — too fast for a human-driven runbook.
scenarios.title: The 60-second RTO
scenarios.why: Fast-Start Failover: the Observer process monitors primary/standby health and auto-promotes the standby when the primary fails (with configurable conditions to avoid flapping). Requires the broker, SYNC-ish transport (max availability/protection), and careful fencing to prevent split-brain. Automation buys speed; it demands rigorous testing.

choices: Active Data Guard — real-time query offload to the physical standby while redo apply continues; also enables block-change tracking offload and fast incremental backups
Open the standby read-write — it stays a standby
scenarios.hint: Which licensed option lets a physical standby serve queries while staying a standby?
scenarios.prompt: How do you run reports on the standby without breaking DR?
scenarios.situation: Reporting queries hammer the primary. The team has a physical standby sitting idle and asks if it can help.
scenarios.title: The idle standby
scenarios.why: Active Data Guard (licensed option) opens the physical standby read-only while redo apply continues — real-time reporting offload with fresh data, plus DML redirection and offloaded backups. Without ADG, a physical standby is mounted-but-closed (no queries). It's the sanctioned way to monetize the DR investment.

scenarios.title: The lag
scenarios.situation: Apply lag growing.
choices: Investigate transport/apply — lag is the SLA metric
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Growing lag means the standby falls behind — diagnose transport vs apply bottlenecks.

scenarios.title: The untested DR
scenarios.situation: Standby never switched over.
choices: Untested DR fails — drill switchovers regularly
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A never-tested standby is a hypothesis — switchover drills prove it.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Oracle Db as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Architecture Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Architecture is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Architecture?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Architecture issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Architecture is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Architecture supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Architecture failure in Oracle Db.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
evidence: All Architecture components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.situation: Users report that Installation & Creation is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Installation & Creation?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Installation & Creation issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Installation & Creation is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Installation & Creation supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Installation & Creation failure in Oracle Db.

scenarios.title: The ROWNUM trap
scenarios.situation: SELECT with ROWNUM and ORDER BY misbehaves.
choices: Order in a subquery, then apply ROWNUM — or use FETCH FIRST
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. ROWNUM applies before ORDER BY — subquery the sort first, or use FETCH FIRST (12c+).

scenarios.title: The silent exception
scenarios.situation: Code has WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL.
choices: Swallows all errors — silent corruption; handle specifically and log
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL hides every failure — the classic PL/SQL sin.

scenarios.title: The slow loop
scenarios.situation: Row-by-row inserts take hours.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Bulk binds turn hours into minutes — the PL/SQL performance lever.

scenarios.title: The hard parses
scenarios.situation: Library cache contention; no binds.
choices: Bind variables — share cursors, stop hard parsing
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Literal SQL hard-parses every execution — binds let cursors share.

scenarios.title: The stale stats
scenarios.situation: Plan flipped overnight.
choices: Optimizer statistics — stale stats mislead the optimizer
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Sudden plan changes usually mean stale or changed statistics — gather and compare.

scenarios.title: The deadlock
scenarios.situation: ORA-00060 errors.
choices: Redesign: consistent lock order, shorter transactions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Deadlocks signal design issues — order locks consistently, shorten transactions.

scenarios.title: The trigger maze
scenarios.situation: 100 undocumented triggers.
choices: Audit all — document, test, remove dead ones
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Trigger sprawl is tech debt — audit, document, and prune systematically.

scenarios.title: The plug
scenarios.situation: Move a PDB to a new CDB.
choices: Unplug (XML), copy files, plug in — check compatibility first
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unplug/plug with the XML manifest — DBMS_PDB compatibility check first.

scenarios.title: The noisy PDB
scenarios.situation: One PDB starves others.
choices: Resource Manager plan — cap CPU/IO per PDB
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. PDB-level resource caps enforce fairness — the multitenant noisy-neighbor fix.

scenarios.title: The patch win
scenarios.situation: 20 PDBs need patching.
choices: Patch the CDB once — all PDBs benefit
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Multitenant's efficiency: one CDB patch covers every PDB.

scenarios.title: The charset block
scenarios.situation: Plug fails: charset mismatch.
choices: Check compatibility upfront — charsets must align
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Character set compatibility gates plugging — verify with DBMS_PDB before moving.

scenarios.title: The common user
scenarios.situation: App uses C##ADMIN everywhere.
choices: Local users per PDB — least privilege, tenancy-aware
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Common users span PDBs — applications should use local users with minimal grants.

scenarios.title: The canary
scenarios.situation: Upgrade 30 PDBs.
choices: Canary: upgrade one PDB's path first, then roll
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Test the upgrade path on one PDB before committing all thirty.

scenarios.title: The lockdown
scenarios.situation: PDB needs restricted capabilities.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Lockdown profiles constrain what a PDB can do — apply per tenancy needs.

scenarios.title: The interconnect
scenarios.situation: RAC is slow; interconnect saturated.
choices: Faster dedicated interconnect + workload partitioning — reduce cross-node traffic
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Interconnect saturation means blocks ping between nodes — faster fabric and partitioning fix it.

scenarios.title: The split brain
scenarios.situation: Network partition; both sides write.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Quorum via voting disks ensures only one partition survives — fencing is the mechanism.

scenarios.title: The node loss
scenarios.situation: A RAC node dies mid-transaction.
choices: TAF/services fail over — surviving nodes continue
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. RAC's HA promise: services relocate, TAF replays — design apps for it.

scenarios.title: The patch
scenarios.situation: Patch a 4-node RAC.
choices: Rolling — one node at a time, services relocate, zero downtime
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Rolling patches are RAC's operational reward — plan the sequence.

scenarios.title: The hot block
scenarios.situation: One block pinged between nodes constantly.
choices: Partition the workload — affinity reduces Cache Fusion traffic
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Hot-block pinging is a partitioning problem — give hot data node affinity.

scenarios.title: The direct connect
scenarios.situation: App connects to node IPs directly.
choices: Services — logical names with failover and balancing
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Direct node connections bypass RAC's HA — services are the abstraction.

scenarios.title: The RAC question
scenarios.situation: HA needed, no scale-out.
choices: Data Guard — simpler and cheaper for HA alone
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. RAC's complexity needs justification — Data Guard covers HA-only needs.

scenarios.title: The default
scenarios.situation: SCOTT/TIGER still works.
choices: Lock/remove default accounts — the first finding, always
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Default credentials are audit finding #1 — lock or remove them immediately.

scenarios.title: The backup tape
scenarios.situation: Unencrypted backup tapes lost.
choices: Encrypt RMAN backups — tapes are breach vectors
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Backup encryption is non-negotiable — lost media must be unreadable.

scenarios.title: The DBA eyes
scenarios.situation: DBAs can read salary tables.
choices: Database Vault realms — separation of duty
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Vault realms block even privileged users from app data — the insider control.

scenarios.title: The cleartext
scenarios.situation: Traffic between app and DB is plaintext.
choices: Native network encryption / TLS — encrypt in transit
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. In-transit encryption is a checkbox — plaintext is negligent.

scenarios.title: The unaudited
scenarios.situation: No audit trail for salary changes.
choices: Unified audit policy on sensitive tables — capture and review
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Sensitive data needs audit policies — and scheduled reviews.

scenarios.title: The stale CPU
scenarios.situation: No patches in 2 years.
choices: Apply CPUs quarterly — known CVEs are exploited
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Quarterly CPU patching is the routine — stale means vulnerable.

scenarios.title: The SYSDBA
scenarios.situation: Everyone has SYSDBA.
choices: Break-glass only — audit every use, narrow immediately
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. SYSDBA is the keys to the kingdom — break-glass with auditing, never routine.

scenarios.title: The analyze
scenarios.situation: Upgrade planned; no pre-checks.
choices: AutoUpgrade analyze — find blockers before the window
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Pre-upgrade analysis finds the blockers — during the window is too late.

scenarios.title: The downtime
scenarios.situation: Zero-downtime migration required.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. GoldenGate replicates with minimal cutover — the zero-downtime answer.

scenarios.title: The charset
scenarios.situation: Migrating to AL32UTF8.
choices: Scan with CSSCAN/DMU, convert, verify — size for expansion
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Charset migration needs scanning, conversion tooling, and expansion sizing.

scenarios.title: The backout
scenarios.situation: No fallback plan.
choices: Trapped — guaranteed restore points and tested backout required
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Every migration needs a tested way back — hope is not a plan.

scenarios.title: The optimizer
scenarios.situation: Post-upgrade queries slower.
choices: Optimizer behavior changes — compare plans, use SPM baselines
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Upgrades change the optimizer — SQL Plan Management baselines stabilize it.

scenarios.title: The license
scenarios.situation: Moving to cloud; license unclear.
choices: Model BYOL vs included — the money question, before migrating
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Cloud licensing math decides the economics — model it upfront.

scenarios.title: The go-no-go
scenarios.situation: Cutover night; mixed signals.
choices: Pre-defined go/no-go criteria — decide before, not during
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Go/no-go gates decided calmly beat 3am judgment calls.

Crash recovery: on startup, Oracle performs automatic crash recovery: SMON rolls forward committed changes from redo and rolls back uncommitted ones. Lose all copies and the instance can't mount — recovery becomes a rebuild-from-backup exercise.
Background processes: multitenant: one CDB (container database) hosts many PDBs (pluggable databases), sharing one instance/SGA/background processes.
Write-ahead logging: this write-ahead logging means: commit is fast because only redo is forced; datafiles catch up later.
SGA: sizing: SGA for caching, PGA for per-session work areas.
PGA (Program Global Area) is per-server-process: sort areas, hash areas, session cursor state.

lessons.title: Installation & Creation — Core concepts
concepts: DBCA is the supported, standard path: it validates prerequisites, applies templates (including CDB/PDB, sample schemas), sets parameters sensibly, and configures listeners/EM. Response files (silent install) and DBCA templates make builds deterministic: same parameters, same options, every time — and they're version-controllable.

Database creation methods: manual creation (CREATE DATABASE script) is for unusual cases — learning internals, or custom layouts DBCA can't express. DB_BLOCK_SIZE is set at database creation and immutable after.

Installation prerequisites: oracle has hard OS prerequisites: the oracle user and groups (oinstall, dba), kernel parameters for shared memory/semaphores (SHMMAX, SEMMNS etc.), package dependencies, and ulimits.
Character sets: the database character set determines how text is stored; changing it after data exists ranges from restricted (CSSCAN/CSALTER for compatible supersets) to full export/import.

lessons.title: Storage Management — Core concepts
concepts: Tablespace roles: block (smallest, e.g., 8 KB) → extent (set of contiguous blocks allocated at once) → segment (the table/index/partition's extents) → tablespace → datafile. Smallfile (traditional, up to 1024 datafiles per tablespace) is the default and fine for typical sizes.

SYSTEM/SYSAUX: not all 'full' is equal: SYSTEM/SYSAUX full blocks DDL and can wedge the database (page now); TEMP full fails the big queries using it (add tempfile or tune the query); UNDO full stalls DML (add space or reduce batch commit scope).
AUTOEXTEND ON with a sensible MAXSIZE lets datafiles grow with demand while capping runaway growth (a bad load can't fill the disk).

Space management: understanding the hierarchy is what makes space reports readable. Each has different space pressure symptoms: SYSTEM full = can't do DDL; TEMP full = big queries fail; UNDO full = DML stalls.

ASM is Oracle's volume manager/filesystem: it stripes data across disks, mirrors per failure group, and rebalances online when disks are added/removed. Bigfile tablespaces use one datafile (up to ~128 TB depending on block size) — fewer files to manage, ideal for very large databases and ASM.
Storage options: filesystem (or NFS/dNFS) storage is simpler and fine for many cases, but striping/mirroring/redundancy become your problem.

lessons.title: Backup & Recovery — Core concepts
concepts: ARCHIVELOG preserves each filled log (ARCn copies it out), so RMAN can restore the midnight backup and roll forward through archived logs to 1:59 PM.

Point-in-time recovery: that's point-in-time recovery, and it's why production runs ARCHIVELOG. When you can't recover to the present (missing/corrupt logs), you do incomplete recovery: RESTORE, RECOVER UNTIL TIME/SEQUENCE, then OPEN RESETLOGS — which resets the log sequence and starts a new database incarnation.
Restore vs recover: rule: logical error (wrong DML, dropped object) → Flashback (fast, online); physical loss (dead disk, corrupt file) → RMAN restore + recover.

RMAN concepts: manage lifecycle inside RMAN: CONFIGURE RETENTION POLICY (recovery window of N days, or redundancy of N copies), then DELETE OBSOLETE / DELETE EXPIRED to clean catalog + files together.
RMAN media recovery rebuilds physically lost/damaged files from backups + redo. RMAN's catalog tracks every backup piece — OS-level deletes leave phantom catalog entries.

Incremental backups: and backups are Schrödinger's backups until tested: RESTORE VALIDATE checks readability, but only a real test restore proves recoverability. Consequences: take a fresh backup immediately (old backups belong to the prior incarnation), and Data Guard standbys need re-instantiation.

lessons.title: Performance — Core concepts
concepts: AWR: methodology: AWR snapshots capture workload stats over intervals; ADDM analyzes them and ranks findings; ASH samples active sessions every second for fine-grained 'who waited on what'.

Optimizer statistics: the cost-based optimizer chooses plans from statistics (row counts, distinct values, histograms, index clustering). The E-Rows/A-Rows gap is the classic smoking gun: the optimizer estimated 10 rows (nested loops looked cheap) but got 2M (nested loops = disaster).
DBMS_STATS.GATHER_* refreshes them; check DBA_TAB_STATISTICS.LAST_ANALYZED.
Execution plans: read plans inside-out: driving table, access path, join method, then row estimates.

lessons.title: Data Guard Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Physical standby: active Data Guard (licensed option) opens the physical standby read-only while redo apply continues — real-time reporting offload with fresh data, plus DML redirection and offloaded backups.

Logical standby = SQL apply into open tables, read-write — usable for reporting and even rolling upgrades, but it's a logical reconstruction, not a block copy. Failover: primary is gone — promote the standby, accept possible data loss (depends on protection mode/sync), one-way.
Switchover: coordinated, both databases healthy — primary becomes standby and vice versa, zero data loss, used for maintenance/patching.
Failover: fast-Start Failover: the Observer process monitors primary/standby health and auto-promotes the standby when the primary fails (with configurable conditions to avoid flapping).
Protection modes: max Protection: SYNC with guarantee — primary stalls rather than risk loss (highest safety, availability cost).

Redo transport: monitor transport lag (redo shipped vs generated) and apply lag (redo applied vs received) via V$DATAGUARD_STATS / Data Guard Broker. Max Performance: ASYNC redo — primary never waits, standby may lag (potential loss).

example.code:

Reasoning: Physical standby = redo apply, block-identical, mounted (read-only with Active Data Guard) — the true DR replica for failover.
Takeaway: Max Performance: ASYNC redo — primary never waits, standby may lag (potential loss).

lessons.title: Oracle Database - Core concepts
concepts: An Oracle instance is memory plus processes; the database is the files. The SGA (buffer cache, shared pool, redo log buffer) is shared memory, background processes like DBWn and LGWR do the writing, and datafiles, control files, and the parameter file persist everything.

Multitenant architecture packs many pluggable databases (PDBs) into one container database (CDB). You patch and back up once at the CDB level while each PDB stays logically isolated - and cloning a PDB is the fastest way to provision dev and test copies.

Every change generates redo (the journal for recovery) and undo (the before-image for rollback and read consistency). Run production in ARCHIVELOG mode so redo is preserved and any point in time is recoverable.

RMAN is the supported backup tool: it understands Oracle block structure, so it can take incremental backups, skip unused blocks, and validate backups. Back up archivelogs too, or the recovery area fills and the database stalls.

Tune with evidence: AWR snapshots and ASH show where DB time goes via wait events. Match the top wait to its cause - scattered reads mean full scans, sequential reads mean index I/O - and fix the plan before buying hardware.

example.walkthrough: Connect as SYSDBA and check two fundamentals in one pass: every PDB's open mode (is the application's database actually open?) and the log mode (is point-in-time recovery even possible?). Make this your first check on any unfamiliar database.

pitfalls: Common trap: saying 'the database is down' when only the listener is down - the instance and data are fine; test with a local sqlplus connection before escalating.
Common trap: trusting a backup that has never been restored - schedule test restores; a backup log saying 'completed' is not proof of recoverability.
Common trap: running NOARCHIVELOG in production to 'save space' - the first media failure becomes data loss back to the last backup.
Common trap: tuning by enlarging the SGA for every slow query - check the execution plan and top wait events first; most slow SQL is a plan problem, not a memory problem.

simulations.brief: The database is in NOARCHIVELOG mode and last night's backup failed. The business needs point-in-time recovery capability by Friday.
simulations.debrief: NOARCHIVELOG means no point-in-time recovery — only whole cold backups. The fix is enabling ARCHIVELOG (requires a restart), then taking a full backup as the new baseline. Never promise PITR without archived redo.

evidence: Last successful backup: 9 days ago; last night: failed — media full
steps.explain: Two problems: NOARCHIVELOG mode makes point-in-time recovery impossible, and the backup media is full. The recovery strategy must fix both: free or add media, enable ARCHIVELOG, then take a full baseline backup.

sections.heading: Architecture
items: Instance — Instance = memory (SGA) + background processes; database = physical files (datafiles, control files, redo logs). The control file is the database's metadata hub: datafile/tempfile locations, log sequence numbers, checkpoint SCN, RMAN repository info.

Crash recovery — on startup, Oracle performs automatic crash recovery: SMON rolls forward committed changes from redo and rolls back uncommitted ones. Lose all copies and the instance can't mount — recovery becomes a rebuild-from-backup exercise.
Background processes — multitenant: one CDB (container database) hosts many PDBs (pluggable databases), sharing one instance/SGA/background processes.
Write-ahead logging — this write-ahead logging means: commit is fast because only redo is forced; datafiles catch up later.
SGA — sizing: SGA for caching, PGA for per-session work areas.
PGA (Program Global Area) is per-server-process — sort areas, hash areas, session cursor state.
Common trap — multitenant requires a separate license for every PDB in all editions.
Common trap — PGA is shared across sessions for efficiency.
Common trap — the database is corrupted; restore from backup.
Common trap — datafiles are gone when the instance dies.

sections.heading: Installation & Creation
items: DBCA is the supported, standard path — it validates prerequisites, applies templates (including CDB/PDB, sample schemas), sets parameters sensibly, and configures listeners/EM. Response files (silent install) and DBCA templates make builds deterministic: same parameters, same options, every time…

Database creation methods — manual creation (CREATE DATABASE script) is for unusual cases — learning internals, or custom layouts DBCA can't express. DB_BLOCK_SIZE is set at database creation and immutable after.

Installation prerequisites — oracle has hard OS prerequisites: the oracle user and groups (oinstall, dba), kernel parameters for shared memory/semaphores (SHMMAX, SEMMNS etc.), package dependencies, and ulimits.
Character sets — the database character set determines how text is stored; changing it after data exists ranges from restricted (CSSCAN/CSALTER for compatible supersets) to full export/import.
Common trap — character sets can be changed anytime with ALTER DATABASE.
Common trap — kernel parameters are set automatically on all platforms.
Common trap — NLS settings don't affect stored data.
Common trap — creation success message is sufficient proof.

sections.heading: Storage Management
items: Tablespace roles — block (smallest, e.g., 8 KB) → extent (set of contiguous blocks allocated at once) → segment (the table/index/partition's extents) → tablespace → datafile. Smallfile (traditional, up to 1024 datafiles per tablespace) is the default and fine for typical sizes.

SYSTEM/SYSAUX — not all 'full' is equal: SYSTEM/SYSAUX full blocks DDL and can wedge the database (page now); TEMP full fails the big queries using it (add tempfile or tune the query); UNDO full stalls DML (add space or reduce batch commit scope).
AUTOEXTEND ON — AUTOEXTEND ON with a sensible MAXSIZE lets datafiles grow with demand while capping runaway growth (a bad load can't fill the disk).

Space management — understanding the hierarchy is what makes space reports readable. Each has different space pressure symptoms: SYSTEM full = can't do DDL; TEMP full = big queries fail; UNDO full = DML stalls.

ASM is Oracle's volume manager/filesystem — it stripes data across disks, mirrors per failure group, and rebalances online when disks are added/removed. Bigfile tablespaces use one datafile (up to ~128 TB depending on block size) — fewer files to manage, ideal for very large databases and ASM.
Storage options — filesystem (or NFS/dNFS) storage is simpler and fine for many cases, but striping/mirroring/redundancy become your problem.
Common trap — space alerts are unnecessary with AUTOEXTEND.
Common trap — one giant datafile per tablespace is best practice.
Common trap — disable AUTOEXTEND everywhere and extend manually at 3 AM.
Common trap — space issues resolve themselves.

sections.heading: Backup & Recovery
items: ARCHIVELOG — ARCHIVELOG preserves each filled log (ARCn copies it out), so RMAN can restore the midnight backup and roll forward through archived logs to 1:59 PM.

Point-in-time recovery — that's point-in-time recovery, and it's why production runs ARCHIVELOG. When you can't recover to the present (missing/corrupt logs), you do incomplete recovery: RESTORE, RECOVER UNTIL TIME/SEQUENCE, then OPEN RESETLOGS — which resets the log sequence and s…
Restore vs recover — rule: logical error (wrong DML, dropped object) → Flashback (fast, online); physical loss (dead disk, corrupt file) → RMAN restore + recover.

RMAN concepts — manage lifecycle inside RMAN: CONFIGURE RETENTION POLICY (recovery window of N days, or redundancy of N copies), then DELETE OBSOLETE / DELETE EXPIRED to clean catalog + files together.
RMAN — RMAN media recovery rebuilds physically lost/damaged files from backups + redo. RMAN's catalog tracks every backup piece — OS-level deletes leave phantom catalog entries.

Incremental backups — and backups are Schrödinger's backups until tested: RESTORE VALIDATE checks readability, but only a real test restore proves recoverability. Consequences: take a fresh backup immediately (old backups belong to the prior incarnation), and Data Guard standbys…
Common trap — recover copies files; restore applies logs.
Common trap — ARCHIVELOG mode slows down commits unacceptably.
Common trap — NOARCHIVELOG is fine for production; backups are enough.
Common trap — cumulative incrementals don't exist in RMAN.

sections.heading: Performance
items: AWR — methodology: AWR snapshots capture workload stats over intervals; ADDM analyzes them and ranks findings; ASH samples active sessions every second for fine-grained 'who waited on what'.

Optimizer statistics — the cost-based optimizer chooses plans from statistics (row counts, distinct values, histograms, index clustering). The E-Rows/A-Rows gap is the classic smoking gun: the optimizer estimated 10 rows (nested loops looked cheap) but got 2M (nested loops = disa…
DBMS_STATS.GATHER_ — DBMS_STATS.GATHER_* refreshes them; check DBA_TAB_STATISTICS.LAST_ANALYZED.
Execution plans — read plans inside-out: driving table, access path, join method, then row estimates.
Common trap — the optimizer doesn't use statistics.
Common trap — restart the database; performance issues are usually transient.
Common trap — plans are unreadable; just try hints.
Common trap — gathering stats always makes things worse.

The E-Rows/A-Rows gap is the classic smoking gun — the optimizer estimated 10 rows (nested loops looked cheap) but got 2M (nested loops = disaster). Root cause is almost always bad/missing stats or missing histograms. Fix the inputs (stats), not the plan — hints freeze a plan that may rot.

sections.heading: Data Guard Basics
items: Physical standby — active Data Guard (licensed option) opens the physical standby read-only while redo apply continues — real-time reporting offload with fresh data, plus DML redirection and offloaded backups.

Logical standby = SQL apply into open tables, read-write — usable for reporting and even rolling upgrades, but it's a logical reconstruction, not a block copy. Failover: primary is gone — promote the standby, accept possible data loss (depends on protection mode/sync), one-way.
Switchover — coordinated, both databases healthy — primary becomes standby and vice versa, zero data loss, used for maintenance/patching.
Failover — fast-Start Failover: the Observer process monitors primary/standby health and auto-promotes the standby when the primary fails (with configurable conditions to avoid flapping).
Protection modes — max Protection: SYNC with guarantee — primary stalls rather than risk loss (highest safety, availability cost).

Redo transport — monitor transport lag (redo shipped vs generated) and apply lag (redo applied vs received) via V$DATAGUARD_STATS / Data Guard Broker. Max Performance: ASYNC redo — primary never waits, standby may lag (potential loss).
Common trap — automatic failover is the default in Data Guard.
Common trap — the modes only affect speed, not data loss.
Common trap — physical standby accepts writes.
Common trap — failover is planned; switchover is emergency.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
